items.title: 克里米亚大桥再遭袭，普京称将“痛苦得多”报复
items.summary: 据英国广播公司报道，连接俄罗斯与克里米亚的克里米亚大桥本周第三次遭袭，周四凌晨铁路桥段被击中，列车服务一度中断，下午恢复，公路交通则在可预见时间内禁止通行。乌克兰称袭击使用“海王星”巡航导弹，俄交通部称无人受伤。俄罗斯总统普京在深圳三方会谈后的记者会上表示，莫斯科的报复将比乌方袭击“痛苦得多”，并称大桥仅用于民用目的。乌克兰国防部称，这些打击为乌方“赢得了时间、拯救了生命”。

Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this week

ByLaura Gozzi

Updated 11 minutes ago

Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.

In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.

A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.

But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November

Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.

Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."

The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.

The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.

It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.

Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.

Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.

• Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by UkrainePublished1 day ago

In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.

Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.

This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

items.title: IMF总裁警告AI需求将推高全球利率
items.summary: 国际货币基金组织（IMF）总裁格奥尔基耶娃警告，对人工智能的旺盛需求将迫使全球主要央行加息。据卫报报道，她在深圳举行的2026年亚太经合组织会议上表示，AI硬件及相关技术产品需求正推高各国消费价格，加上中东战争带来的能源冲击，将使今年全球通胀升至4.7%，这要求许多经济体收紧货币政策。她还称，AI硬件及相关产品已占全球商品贸易的十分之一以上。

Kristalina Georgieva told the Apec summit that while the impact of war in the Middle East would eventually dissipate, ‘AI is forever’. Photograph: Ng Han Guan/AFP/Getty Images

AI demand will push up interest rates around the world, IMF head warns

Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’

• Business live – latest updates

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab

Read more

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Central banks have been forced to raise interest rates this year after the outbreak of war in February drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel, reigniting inflationary pressures around the world. The European Central Bank raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month.

Financial markets expect further increases in the cost of borrowing next year, as the rapid rollout of AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of the conflict.

However, global oil prices have fallen back in recent weeks, following the US midterm elections and an upswing in the supply of crude. Fears about an AI bubble and febrile conditions in global equity markets could dent business investment, and economists warn of a slowdown in demand as high inflation squeezes households.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

items.title: 以军越过“黄线”进入加沙中部，称行动已完成
items.summary: 据卫报报道，以色列军队周三越过“黄线”进入哈马斯控制的加沙中部，这是去年10月停火协议达成以来首次跨线地面行动，坦克沿加沙主要南北通道萨拉赫丁公路行进，迫使数十名流离失所的巴勒斯坦人逃离帐篷。以军发言人称行动针对“黄线”以西的哈马斯基础设施，持续约24小时，周四宣布“已完成”。哈马斯谴责此举是“对停火协议的公然违反”。巴勒斯坦医护人员称，以军空袭造成一人死亡。

Displaced Palestinian people in Nuseirat evacuate from tent shelters with their belongings amid an Israeli military incursion into the area, the first to cross the ‘yellow line’ since the fragile ceasefire was agreed last October. Photograph: Eyad Baba/AFP/Getty Images

Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza

First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu

The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.

An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The military ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

Children at risk as ‘weaponisation of aid’ surges in conflict zones, analysis finds

Read more

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.

Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.

Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.

Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.

Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

Read more

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.

Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

items.title: 丹麦议会一致通过格陵兰安全协议
items.summary: 丹麦议会周四以109票赞成、0票反对一致批准丹麦、格陵兰与美国之间的北极安全协议。据卫报报道，该协议由美国总统特朗普与格陵兰自治政府总理尼尔森、丹麦首相弗雷泽里克森于9月签署，更新1951年防务协定，给予美国在格陵兰的水下通行权及建设导弹防御系统的具体许可，并承认格陵兰为平等伙伴。丹麦外交大臣拉斯穆森称协议“消除了围绕格陵兰的所有不确定性”，但警告对美信任需要重建。美国驻丹麦大使豪厄里称这是“历史性”协议。

The Greenlandic MPs Naaja Nathanielsen (sitting) and Qarsoq Høegh-Dam (waving) during the proceedings in parliament on Thursday. Photograph: Mads Claus Rasmussen/EPA

Danish MPs approve Greenland security pact with US

Danish foreign minister says deal ‘removes all uncertainty’ over territory but warns trust in US needs rebuilding

• Europe live – latest updates

The Danish parliament has unanimously approved a new Arctic security pact between Greenland, Denmark and the US in what it is hoped will mark a new chapter in relations, months after Donald Trump’s threats to invade the largely autonomous territory.

The deal, which was signed by the US president and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen, in September after months of talks, updates a 1951 defence agreement to give the US underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system.

It also recognises Greenland, a former Danish colony, as an equal partner and stipulates that if it were to become fully independent of Denmark, it would remain in Nato.

Having already been approved by the Greenlandic parliament earlier this month, all that remains for the agreement to come into effect, said the Danish foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, is for Trump to send a notification to the US Congress.

“We have now resolved our part of the equation,” Løkke Rasmussen said after the bill was passed. “This is a positive development, as it removes all uncertainty surrounding Greenland and establishes a proper framework for future cooperation.”

But he warned that trust with the US had been damaged. “Consequently, there is a significant task of rebuilding ahead. But this will take place within the framework of an agreement, which is a good thing,” he said.

Before the deal was signed, Trump said the US would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland”. But Løkke Rasmussen said on Thursday that the US was yet to inform Denmark of any plans to establish new military bases.

The US ambassador to Denmark, Ken Howery, said on social media he was “thrilled that the Danish parliament today voted unanimously 109-0 to ratify the Greenland security agreement”.

In a statement, he said: “On behalf of the United States, I welcome the strong support in Denmark’s parliament for the ratification of the historic US-Denmark-Greenland defence agreement, paving the way for it to enter into force.

“The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernises our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of Nato.”

He added: “Thank you to colleagues in Denmark and Greenland for the many hours spent negotiating the agreement, which makes us safer, stronger and more secure. I look forward to continuing our work to deepen our cooperation as we implement the agreement and advance other shared priorities with our friends and allies throughout the kingdom of Denmark.”

Relations between the US and Denmark and Greenland – and the Nato alliance as a whole – had come under unprecedented strain amid repeated threats by Trump to take over the Arctic territory that led to Denmark preparing for a US invasion.

Such was the perceived threat in January that Copenhagen reportedly sent over blood bags, and explosives to blow up runways, in case of US attack.

items.summary: 国际法院（ICJ）周四裁定，缅甸在2016至2017年的军事行动中对罗兴亚少数民族实施了种族灭绝，这是该法院首次认定一国犯有种族灭绝罪。据卫报报道，法院院长岩泽雄司称，15名法官中有9人认为缅甸“对罗兴亚人实施了种族灭绝”，并呼吁缅甸提供赔偿和恢复原状，包括让罗兴亚人安全返回家园。该案由冈比亚代表罗兴亚幸存者提起，审理历时七年。据南华早报报道，2017年的镇压造成至少1万人死亡。卫报称，2016至2017年的军事行动迫使逾70万罗兴亚人越境逃往孟加拉国。

A man helps Rohingya Muslim refugees to disembark from a boat on the Bangladeshi shoreline of the Naf River after crossing the border from Myanmar in September 2017. Photograph: Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images

Myanmar committed acts of genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

Judgment ends seven-year legal battle and is seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of all state crimes

Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya minority during “clearance operations” nearly a decade ago, the world’s highest court has ruled.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle and is seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

“The court is fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar,” the ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said during a reading of the judgment.

A 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, with refugees arriving with stories of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Governments have been anxiously awaiting the decision, handed down in The Hague, the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Myanmar’s case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than 1 million Rohingya still live there in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Mumtaz Begum, pictured in 2017 in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She fled to Bangladesh shortly after an attack on Tula Toli village in Myanmar, in which she said the military burned homes, gang-raped women and killed her husband and son in front of her. Photograph: Allison Joyce/Getty Images

Refugees who fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

Myanmar denied carrying out a genocide and claims its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

Bangladeshi guards stand by as thousands of Rohingya refugees fleeing from Myanmar walk along a muddy rice field after crossing the border in Palang Khali, Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Paula Bronstein/Getty Images

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges might assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

A Myanmar border guard police stands near a fence, behind which are Rohingya refugees and makeshift houses at the ‘no man’s land’ zone between the Bangladesh-Myanmar border in Rakhine State, western Myanmar, in 2018. Photograph: Nyein Chan Naing/EPA

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkans wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

items.summary: 人工智能公司Anthropic周四在纽约上市，募资810亿美元，创下首次公开募股纪录。据英国广播公司报道，股份定价为每股83美元，高于此前70至78美元的区间，公司估值约1.5万亿美元，成为全球市值最高的公司之一。公司截至今年9月的九个月营收达330亿美元，同期净亏损1040亿美元。据半岛电视台报道，投资者认购需求达发行量的六倍，公司售出9.8亿股，高于原计划的8.25亿股，股票代码为“ANT”。

Figure caption,

Who are the investors ready to jump on Anthropic?

ByKali Hays, Technology reporter, Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent and Osmond Chia, Business reporter

Updated 1 hour ago

Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62.bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The firm's $1.5tn valuation makes it more valuable than Walmart and Samsung and on almost on a par with Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

Crucial test for AI

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Rapid rise

Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.

Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.

The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.

OpenAI has voiced similar sentiments and delayed its plans to list on the stock market in order to address AI safety concerns.

Image source, Getty Images

Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.

But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."

Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.

Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.

Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.

And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance

Updated November 19, 20266:08 AM ET

Originally published November 19, 20264:44 AM ET

Heard on Morning Edition

By

Charles Maynes

,

Jennifer Pak

,

Deepa Shivaram

Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance

Listen

<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6040432/nx-s1-10011091" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

President Donald Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China.

Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP

hide caption

Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP

SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday. Their meeting capped two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.

"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," Xi said in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."

Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."

RIYADH: A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday (Nov 19), witnesses told AFP, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighbouring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

In the early hours of Thursday, AFP journalists in the Saudi capital reported a powerful blast had been heard.

Around the same time, civil defence authorities issued a warning for "potential danger" but said minutes later that the danger had passed.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had "addressed a missile threat launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh".

"Initial assessment indicates the impact of debris, with material damage currently being surveyed," said coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki.

Witnesses later told AFP that Riyadh's Public Investment Fund Tower, which at 80 storeys is the tallest in the city's financial district, had been damaged.

"The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out," said one source who requested anonymity. Two other sources confirmed the damage.

Standing 385 metres high, the tower dominates King Abdullah Financial District, which acts as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions.

With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.

Chaired by Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest in the world with more than US$900 billion in assets under management.

It is also one of the main instruments for diversifying the kingdom's economy away from oil, plans which have been threatened by the latest fighting.

Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of anti-Houthi coalition: state media

Gulf nations attacked after US strikes Iranian island

DEADLY AIRPORT ATTACK

Malki also said Thursday that the coalition had intercepted five ballistic missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia's southern region, which borders Yemen.

The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking targets including airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh's financial district.

In October, a deadly attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.

In response, the Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi targets in areas of Yemen held by the group.

On Thursday, Houthi media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had launched another attack on Yemen's capital Sanaa.

The Almasirah television channel said Saudi forces have "once again targeted the shoe and textile factory of the Alyateem Development Foundation", citing its correspondent in Sanaa.

The Saudi coalition said it had "destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar", a city about 100km south of Sanaa that was used by the Houthis to strike Riyadh.

People walk on the debris of a shoe and textile factory in the al-Nahda neighbourhood of al-Thawra district following an airstrike in Sanaa, Yemen, on Nov 17, 2026. (Photo: AP)

CROWN PRINCE MEETING

The long-running civil war in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, fell dormant in 2022 after a ceasefire was implemented, but sprang back to life this summer.

The Houthis are now nearing Aden, the internationally recognised government's interim capital, having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed.

More than 1,600 people have been killed in the latest round of fighting and more than 300,000 displaced, according to the United Nations.

On Thursday, the Saudi crown prince met with US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh, according to state news agency SPA.

The two sides "reviewed bilateral relations, particularly in the military fields, and discussed regional developments", the media outlet said.

On Wednesday, another powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh, with residents saying no mobile phone alerts were issued beforehand, as is usually the case.

"The explosion was extremely loud," said one resident in the north of the city. "Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening."

The coalition said it had intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis in the Riyadh and southern regions.

The military spokesman for the Houthis, Yahya Saree, said in a post on X that the group had targeted Riyadh's international airport and the capital's financial district with cruise missiles.

PARIS: The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the "largest threat" to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on Thursday (Nov 19).

The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave "lasting marks", the agency warned.

Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February.

Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel - which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments - supply lines remain severely disrupted.

"The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report.

He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets.

"Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply," Birol wrote.

The report said elsewhere that "increasingly it is falling to consumers - and high prices - to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down".

Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from "several cushioning factors".

How exposed is Southeast Asia’s energy supply to the Iran war - who is most vulnerable and what’s next?

What the Iran war shows about Singapore's energy resilience for now and the future

"NO PATHWAY" BACK

The IEA's report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal.

The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at "stated" government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050.

In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035.

For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists.

"While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be," Birol said in a press release.

"And I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before."

Source: AFP/ia

PARIS: The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the "largest threat" to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on Thursday (Nov 19).

The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave "lasting marks", the agency warned.

Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February.

Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel - which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments - supply lines remain severely disrupted.

"The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report.

He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets.

"Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply," Birol wrote.

The report said elsewhere that "increasingly it is falling to consumers - and high prices - to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down".

Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from "several cushioning factors".
How exposed is Southeast Asia’s energy supply to the Iran war - who is most vulnerable and what’s next?
What the Iran war shows about Singapore's energy resilience for now and the future
"NO PATHWAY" BACK

The IEA's report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal.

The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at "stated" government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050.

In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035.

For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists.

"While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be," Birol said in a press release.

"And I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before."

Jay Clayton arrives to testify before a Senate intelligence committee confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington DC on 15 July 2026. Photograph: Nathan Howard/Reuters

US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages

As Democrats flag AI bank breaches and cyber-attacks in Japan, Jay Clayton says system failures happen

• US politics live – latest updates

A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies.

Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more.

“The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” Cantwell and Rounds wrote to Clayton, who is also serving as the White House AI czar.

“Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services,” the senators wrote.

Over the last week, tech outages at major banks, workplace communication systems and even federal infrastructure like the Federal Aviation Administration – triggering a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that grounded or delayed thousands of flights – have raised alarms about potential cyber-attacks.

Top officials have insisted the disruptions stem from software patch updates that intend to address potential AI harms.

Clayton and other national security officials told lawmakers on Wednesday that there was no indication the recent outages were the result of a malicious attack.

“Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said during the House homeland security committee hearing.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, and Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, similarly said they had no reason to believe the outages were connected or the result of an attack.

“Many people are patching their systems. They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated,” Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday. “It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure and as you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happen.”

Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, echoed Clayton. “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” he wrote on X.

Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, attempted to quell public speculation and fear by assuring Americans that the tech outages were not linked to one another or the work of malicious actors.

But nationwide cyber outages have roiled the country, filled with voters who are already skeptical of rapidly integrating and developing AI. It is unclear what exactly has caused the widespread outages or if AI played a role.

JD Vance canceled his scheduled interview at the New York Times’ DealBook summit on Wednesday, citing his need to attend meetings addressing the recent tech outages.

Cantwell and Rounds are asking Clayton to provide cybersecurity tools to critical US infrastructure such as hospitals, utilities, small government, federal agencies and more, to prevent further disruptions.

They are also asking that US cybersecurity teams secure the same AI systems that are deployed to find vulnerabilities in software, raising concerns that they can “gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems”.

Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

ByOlivia Ireland, Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv and Ilya Abishev, BBC News Russian

Updated 12 minutes ago

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.

The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the attack, though he is yet to comment.

Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The Security Service of Ukraine said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".

The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

Image source, EPA

Image caption,

There was heavy traffic in Kyiv on Tuesday after two major crossings were closed after strikes

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

MANILA: President Donald Trump said on Tuesday (Nov 17) that United States authorities take "very seriously" any possible threat to Washington, following reports Iran was planning to target officials, possibly with a radioactive bomb.

Asked about the potential threat during a visit to the Philippines, Trump said: "If there is (such a threat), they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."

"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy."

CNN, citing seven anonymous US officials, reported that US intelligence indicated that Iran was preparing to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb in Washington.

"Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," Baqaei wrote on X.

Negotiations between the US and Iran to end their war have stalled, and Iran recently targeted US infrastructure in the Middle East.

Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank

Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’

• UK politics live – latest updates

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.

The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month.

Miliband announced the measures just before tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement were due to be allocated by the Israeli government, while saying he wanted to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way.

Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot has said that, if appointed, he will take a tougher approach than Benjamin Netanyahu to settler violence.

Eisenkot (left) and Netanyahu at the Knesset on 10 November. Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images

The sanctions are designed to stop the flow of finance to eight identified construction firms, although in practice the extent to which any of the firms are dependent on British finance is yet to be tested.

On 8 September, Miliband announced an expansion of its Global Human Rights sanctions regime, as well as a complex set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. The Foreign Office said that it welcomed and encouraged trade with “green line Israel” and firmly distinguished this with activity in settlements.

The Foreign Office said the current Israeli government had “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them”. More settlements had been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years.

The entities targeted by sanctions are Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband – who was criticised by some for broadening the sanctions criteria and planning a ban on trade with illegal settlement – said: “Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.”

Palestinian children at a makeshift school established inside tents in Gaza City. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty Images

‘The cold is lethal’: storms leave thousands in Gaza without shelter

Read more

But he added in a potential olive branch: “We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”

Miliband and his Middle East minister, Stephen Doughty, have repeatedly highlighted the Israeli government’s refusal to let a variety of dual-use goods into Gaza. The Foreign Office said civilians in Gaza were in desperate need of winter supplies, with catastrophic floods leaving nearly 4,000 households without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters.

According to the UN, more than 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins bought by humanitarian partners and donors are outside Gaza ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities. The Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.

The Israeli government claims the blockage of some goods is necessary to prevent Hamas obtaining items that could be used to attack Israel. The dispute over dual-use goods and closed entry points into Gaza has lasted for more than two years.

Image source, Getty Images

ByLauren Turner

BBC News

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

• Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China

In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May

ByOsmond Chia

Business reporter

As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

A blow to Asia's AI boom

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".

A headache for China

The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.

"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.

Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.

The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.

But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, have struck an agreement to reduce some tariffs between their countries, a largely symbolic move that shows relations between the two countries are warming as Canada’s ties to the United States falter.

While the expanded trade between China and Canada resulting from the accord in the Chinese tech and financial hub Shenzhen will be modest, involving just $280 million in exports, the pact — as well as the seemingly amicable meeting — illustrates a contrast to Mr. Carney’s relationship with President Trump. Earlier this year, Mr. Carney said that the United States was “at war” with Canada after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed in acrimony.

Talks are restarting between Canada and the United States but there is no indication that Washington will back away from key irritants including tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.

Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has been traveling the world to diversify Canada’s economic and political ties away from the United States. Those efforts include current talks to make Canada the European Union’s first associate member and Mr. Carney’s second formal meeting this year with Mr. Xi.

“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” Mr. Carney said at the start of the meeting with Mr. Xi on Tuesday.

He added that Canada is ahead of schedule with its goal of a 50 percent increase in exports to China by the end of the decade.

items.summary: 据卫报报道，英国国家统计局数据显示，9月失业率意外降至4.6%，低于8月的4.7%和今年早些时候的5%；截至9月底三个月的剔除奖金薪资增速降至3.5%。职位空缺10月降至69万个，为2014年以来最低，英国商会称这一水平“令人担忧”，18至24岁失业率达13%，接近成年人平均水平的近三倍。同日，艾伦·米尔本发布青年就业报告，他称其计划每年仅能为政府节省2亿英镑。

UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6%, as government prepares to release Milburn report

Wage growth falls to to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work

• Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

• Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release a major report on the youth jobs crisis.

The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had expected it to remain at 4.7%.

However, wage growth fell to 3.5%, excluding bonuses, in the latest official figures for the three months to the end of September, down from 3.7% in the three months to August.

Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

Read more

With inflation also at 3.5% and expected to rise for a fourth consecutive month to 3.7% when figures are released on Wednesday, the average worker faces a fall in real wages growth to zero or even into negative territory.

The figures highlighted how difficult it will be for ministers to improve living standards as they consider the findings of a key report by the former health secretary Alan Milburn examining how to get young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) back into work, released later on Tuesday.

The jobs market has proved difficult for analysts and politicians to assess in recent years. It has been called weak after a dramatic slide in the number of vacancies, which illustrates the reticence of companies to hire new staff.

However, employment has proved resilient, with unemployment falling between July and August from 4.9% to 4.7%, indicating that few employers were ready to cut large numbers of staff.

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

Read more

Ministers are known to be concerned that some large employers, including several banks, have said they intend to use artificial intelligence to reduce their staffing levels.

Economists are divided over whether AI will enhance productivity across all major sectors of the economy – after signs it has boosted GDP – or lead to improvements in certain industries, such as healthcare.

Employer groups have complained that Labour’s increase in national insurance payments, a higher minimum wage and changes to employee rights have increased costs, leading to a fall in the number of advertised vacancies.

The Bank of England increased interests rates earlier this month after a rise in the consumer prices index to 3.5% in September.

It has said that its own surveys showed employers did not expect to increase pay beyond 3.5% to 4% next year, despite the higher level of inflation, and also reported little change looking ahead in their own prices.

However, a growing number of the Bank’s policymakers believe the prospect of high oil and energy prices next year as the Iran war drags on will push inflation towards 5% and force employers to offer higher pay, which will be passed on in higher retail prices.

By Russ BuettnerKhadija SharifeBrian FitzpatrickFrederik ObermaierBastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann

Nov. 17, 2026

When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.

Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.

At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.

“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”

This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.

But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.

Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year

ByMichael Race and Osmond Chia, Business reporters

Updated 17 November 2026 02:37 GMT

Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.

But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.

The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.

Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.

• The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandalPublished4 days ago

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".

Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley

New rules

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.

The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.

The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.

The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.

Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.

He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".

In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

• How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?Published4 days ago

• How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White HousePublished4 days ago

The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.

The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.

Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.

But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.

But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Figure caption,

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry.

US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.

The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.

'A handshake with Jensen'

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

She has long black hair and a golden earring, and is wearing a sleeveless yellow dress. Both appear to be inside a crowded dark-lit room.
