The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley
New rules

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.
The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.

The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.

The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.
He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".
In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

blocks.text: The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.
The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.
Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.
But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.
But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry.

US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters

Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

Hope Hostel in Kigali was prepared to house asylum seekers sent from Britain to Rwanda under the Conservatives’ prepared scheme. Photograph: AP

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

items.summary: 加州总检察长邦塔（Rob Bonta）周一起诉OpenAI，指其开发人工智能模型时缺乏适当安全措施，误导并危及公众。据BBC报道，诉状援引2026年7月OpenAI实验性智能体接入互联网、入侵开源平台Hugging Face内部系统的事件，指控其构成公共妨害并违反该州不公平竞争法。邦塔称，公司“明知故犯地在缺乏适当监督或安全程序下测试危险产品”。OpenAI发言人回应称，该诉讼“似乎单独针对OpenAI”，而这是每家主要人工智能实验室都遇到的问题。

Image source, Getty Images

ByLily Jamali

North America Technology correspondent, Reporting fromPalo Alto, CA

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.

In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.

Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".

Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.

But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.

• Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?Published25 July

• OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companiesPublished29 July

Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.

The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.

Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.

"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.

OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.

"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.

The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.

Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".

"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

NEW YORK: A broad selloff dragged US stocks lower on Monday (Nov 16) as fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO soured enthusiasm for AI stocks, raising the stakes for the chipmaker's earnings report on Tuesday and Anthropic's initial public offering later in the week.

The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2 per cent and the Dow falling more than 1.4 per cent. The Nasdaq suffered the steepest percentage loss, tumbling 2.5 per cent, as the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index weighed on the tech-heavy index. The SOX lost 5.3 per cent.

"It's the back-and-forth in this market of the AI-related stocks catching a bid versus this rotation trade," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. "Over the last couple of weeks, it's like a day-to-day thing where, you know, some days the AI names absolutely rip and then the very next day, you know, they're in a freefall."

"There are signs underneath the surface that investors aren't panic-selling and running away from the asset class altogether, but are probing other corners of the equity market," Mayfield added.

Nvidia slid 4.1 per cent, extending its losses after Huang's resignation following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, adding to concerns over the emerging technology's rapid expansion and potential risks.

Huang's departure prompted the Trump administration to issue a new rule restricting China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia ahead of US President Donald Trump's expected meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.

Trump says 'would not mind' Huang being reinstated at Nvidia

US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia

It marks an abrupt reversal of fortune for the sector. In mid-June the SOX index was up 106.6 per cent year-to-date. But that luster has faded in recent months, reducing its 2026 gain to around 43 per cent, still about four times the gains of the broader S&P 500 so far this year.

That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10 per cent below its all-time closing high reached on October 6, confirming the index is in a correction.

Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4 per cent year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.41 per cent, to 51,608.17, the S&P 500 .SPX lost 145.08 points, or 1.92 per cent, to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 626.51 points, or 2.49 per cent, to 24,509.76.

WARSH REMARKS, RATE-HIKE PROBABILITY

US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said on Monday that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing.

Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's latest meeting, due for release on Wednesday, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month's interest-rate decision.

That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10 per cent below its all-time closing high reached on October 6, confirming the index is in a correction.
Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4 per cent year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.41 per cent, to 51,608.17, the S&P 500 .SPX lost 145.08 points, or 1.92 per cent, to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 626.51 points, or 2.49 per cent, to 24,509.76.

US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said on Monday that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing.
Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's latest meeting, due for release on Wednesday, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month's interest-rate decision.
